sweep_summary: Barasana-Eduria (bara1380, catalog classification tonal, deciding source Gómez-Imbert 2004-05 Amerindia). All five works with stress in the title are Gómez-Imbert works already known to be about the tone/pitch accent system (three are duplicate Glottolog records of the 2001 ILCAA chapter). its abstract (Semantic Scholar, French) calls Barasana a tone language whose F0 contour is set by autosegmental tone distribution over the metrical grid, with pitch accent a property of the morpheme — consistent with the catalog's tonal/pitch accent coding. (2) The 2001 ILCAA chapter (Kaji ed., ISBN 4872977947, CiNii BA54654809) is print-only; Gómez-Imbert 2004-05 herself calls it 'la mejor presentación tonal' — highest acquisition priority. (3) Cahiers de Grammaire 22 (1997) is not online (ERSS server holds only vols 24-30) and, from how the author cites it, concerns moraic/prosodic structure and segmental processes rather than accent placement — low priority. Additionally read the open Cahiers de Grammaire 24 (1999) paper already held by the project: it states Barasana 'peut être analysé comme un accent tonal à deux mélodies, H et HB' (p. 75) and is 'un accent tonal d'un point de vue typologique' (p. 81), with four root melodies H/HL/LH/LHL (p. 82) — confirms the catalog's classification; it does not supersede the 2004-05 deciding source. OpenAlex could not be reached by automated download throughout; archive.org was offline.

No syllable-counting or weight-based stress rule; the Jones & Jones 'phonemic stress' is the same pitch phenomenon. This confirms the catalog's classification (tonal / tonal-OR-pitch accent).

new_statements.quote: L'A. examine le systeme tonique et accentuel du barasama, langue a tons presentant deux caracteristiques : 1. le contour F0 est determine par des principes autosegmentaux distribuant les tons via la grille metrique, 2. l'accent de hauteur est une propriete du morpheme. Puis l'A. se concentre sur trois constructions dans lesquelles l'accent de hauteur de la tete propositionnelle est supplante par un accent determine par l'element precedent.
new_statements.translation: The author examines the tone and accent system of Barasana, a tone language with two characteristics: 1. the F0 contour is determined by autosegmental principles that distribute tones via the metrical grid, 2. pitch accent is a property of the morpheme. The author then concentrates on three constructions in which the pitch accent of the phrasal head is supplanted by an accent determined by the preceding element.

new_statements.quote: [sec. 1] Barasana is a tone language in which the Fo contour of the word is determined by autosegmental principles distributing high and low tones via the metrical grid. Another general feature is that pitch accent is a property of the morpheme — in several senses. First, each lexical morpheme falls into one of two classes marked by a [H] or [HL] tones. Second, there is no contrast in the location of the tones within a morpheme (modulo initial extrametricality). [sec. 8] Barasana has many of the properties of a classic pitch accent system such as Japanese. ... First, in both languages prominence is marked phonetically by an Fo pitch change rather than by duration or amplitude.

new_statements.relation_note: Same classification as the catalog record (Gomez-Imbert 2004-05: restricted tone system analysable as tone or pitch accent, two tonal specifications, moraic weight without accentual role) and as the Gomez-Imbert 1999 statement held by the project (accent tonal à deux mélodies H/HB, extramétricalité à gauche); adds the explicit metrical statement: culminative word accent = leftmost HL else leftmost H (Khalkha-type 'first heavy else first'), F0 the only correlate of prominence, loanword stress mapped to the accent locus, accentual-domain splitting. No syllable-position or weight-based stress rule independent of the lexical melodies, so nothing contradicts the 'tonal' coding.
new_statements.rule_in_words: No stress system separate from tone. Every lexical morpheme carries one of two pitch accents, [H] or [HL]; a lexically marked class also has an 'extrametrical' low initial mora at the left edge of the word/domain (surface LH, LHL). The mora is the tone-bearing unit. Within a morpheme the accent docks on the leftmost (visible) mora (HL trimoraics surface HLL). At word level one accent is projected culminatively: the leftmost [HL] if any, otherwise the leftmost [H] (i.e. initial), the rest are deleted and the winning tones spread, so every word has exactly one pitch peak. Prominence is realised by F0 only, not duration or amplitude; Spanish/Portuguese loans place the [HL] drop on the source-language stressed syllable. Compounds/specifiers/possessors and tonal verb prefixes shift or replace accents; long words split into two accentual domains, each with its own peak.
new_statements.secondary_stress: None described as such; sec. 7: words long enough to contain three feet split into two Accentual Domains, each with its own pitch peak and possible left-edge extrametricality (e.g. ba(á-(rótí-(~bací-~bí realised with a second peak on the prehodiernal suffix).
new_statements.exceptions: Lexically 'extrametrical' (low) initial moras only at the left edge of a word/domain; toneless monomoraic suffixes vs a few final verbal suffixes that introduce HL (sec. 6.4); post-accenting specifiers, accent copy from pronouns in possessives (two domains), décalage of root accent onto the following morpheme after tonal person prefixes, a 'polar' stabilizer prefix; a residual puzzle in (45) left open.
new_statements.identity_note: Gómez-Imbert & Kenstowicz describe Barasana proper (jebá-~baca, Piraparaná basin, Vaupés; fieldwork by Gómez-Imbert since 1983, consultants Barasana with Tatuyo mothers) = Barasana-Eduria bara1380 / Southern Barasano [bsn]; Eduria is named among the exogamous groups in their fn. 2. Stolte & Stolte describe Northern Barasano = Bará/Waimaja (waim1255, [bao]), Caño Colorado, explicitly a distinct language. Smith's SIL 'barasano del sur' materials (held by the project) are bara1380.

tone_statements.quote: Le parcours de la conjugaison montre deux sortes de lexèmes verbaux: 1) ceux qui se manifestent sous deux contours HH et HB; 2) ceux qui sont toujours BH (voir (5) supra ). Cette constante - et ceci est valable pour tous les lexèmes de la langue - indique qu'il y a une SYL, et une seule par lexème, marquée par une propriété TA. Cette propriété peut être interprétée, soit comme tonale dans le cadre d'un système restreint - il n'y aurait que deux mélodies majeures possibles - soit comme un système d'accent tonal. Nous travaillons dans ce deuxième cadre qui nous permet pour l'instant une meilleure compréhension des données.
tone_statements.translation: The survey of the conjugation shows two kinds of verbal lexemes: 1) those that surface with two contours, HH and HL; 2) those that are always LH (see (5) above). This constant - and it holds for all lexemes of the language - indicates that there is one syllable, and only one per lexeme, marked by a tone-accent (TA) property. This property can be interpreted either as tonal within a restricted system - there would be only two major melodies - or as a pitch-accent system. We work within the second framework, which for now gives us a better understanding of the data.

tone_statements.citation: Jones, Wendell and Jones, Paula (1991). Barasano Syntax. Dallas, Texas: SIL International and University of Texas at Arlington. xv+193 pp.
tone_statements.quote: 1.14. Stress and pitch. Stress is phonemic on the word level, with one primary stress per word. Word stress occurs on the nuclear syllable of a word, combined with features of high pitch, loudness, long vowel, and sometimes a fortis consonant (such as the /d/, in idia (idi.a) 'three'). Prenuclear syllables have lower pitch, followed by the nuclear syllable with high pitch. Postnuclear syllables may have either high pitch or low pitch, depending on the particular morphemes involved. [...] Example (38) demonstrates contrastive word stress. (38) rii 'blood' / rii 'meat' [acute on different syllables; scanned lost the diacritics]. Stress patterns differ from one dialect to another. There are some lexical differences between Barasano and Taiwano, but one of the most prominent differences between the two is stress placement. For example, in Barasano, 'bad' has the stress on the second syllable rohose, whereas in Taiwano the stress is on the first syllable rohose.

tone.quote: 1.14. Stress and pitch. Stress is phonemic on the word level, with one primary stress per word. Word stress occurs on the nuclear syllable of a word, combined with features of high pitch, loudness, long vowel, and sometimes a fortis consonant (such as the /d/, in idia (idi.a) 'three'). Prenuclear syllables have lower pitch, followed by the nuclear syllable with high pitch. Postnuclear syllables may have either high pitch or low pitch, depending on the particular morphemes involved. [...] Example (38) demonstrates contrastive word stress. (38) rii 'blood' / rii 'meat' [acute on different syllables; scanned lost the diacritics]. Stress patterns differ from one dialect to another. There are some lexical differences between Barasano and Taiwano, but one of the most prominent differences between the two is stress placement. For example, in Barasano, 'bad' has the stress on the second syllable rohose, whereas in Taiwano the stress is on the first syllable rohose.

sources.note: The grammar says nothing about word stress or lexical tone. Its only prosodic content is clause-level intonation: seven contours (Cr 1-7) defined by the pitch levels (1 low-low to 5 high-high) of the last two syllables of the clause, assigned by clause type, with optional crescendo/decrescendo and emotional registers (high 4-4 for emphasis/excitement, low 2-2 'con acento fuerte' for anger). The phoneme chart (p. xi, p. 13) lists consonants and vowels only; chapter VII Morfofonémica (p. 81, p. 99) gives only vowel rules. 'Acento' occurs once, in the anger-register remark, not as a stres

sources.quote: Le parcours de la conjugaison montre deux sortes de lexèmes verbaux: 1) ceux qui se manifestent sous deux contours HH et HB; 2) ceux qui sont toujours BH (voir (5) supra ). Cette constante - et ceci est valable pour tous les lexèmes de la langue - indique qu'il y a une SYL, et une seule par lexème, marquée par une propriété TA. Cette propriété peut être interprétée, soit comme tonale dans le cadre d'un système restreint - il n'y aurait que deux mélodies majeures possibles - soit comme un système d'accent tonal. Nous travaillons dans ce deuxième cadre qui nous permet pour l'instant une meilleure compréhension des données.

tone.translation: The survey of the conjugation shows two kinds of verbal lexemes: 1) those that surface with two contours, HH and HL; 2) those that are always LH (see (5) above). This constant - and it holds for all lexemes of the language - indicates that there is one syllable, and only one per lexeme, marked by a tone-accent (TA) property. This property can be interpreted either as tonal within a restricted system - there would be only two major melodies - or as a pitch-accent system. We work within the second framework, which for now gives us a better understanding of the data.
